 November 18, 2026 
 Opinion 
 We need to begin mourning AO3
 Illustration by Lauren Smith. 
 Maritza Baptiste , Staff Writer 
 Archive of Our Own, commonly known as AO3, is a nonprofit website dedicated to preserving and publishing fanfiction and various forms of fanwork. The archive has cultivated a reputation as a relatively welcoming creative space where writers can share their work, receive positive feedback and connect with like-minded readers.  
 Its nonprofit structure and commitment to preserving creative freedom distinguishes it from many other fanwork platforms. Writers are not competing for algorithmic visibility, monetizing their work or chasing fame that dominates other social platforms. They are solely focused on a consumer-friendly interface and content published for personal enjoyment.  
 To the dismay of users, AO3 has shut down. Again. This time, however, the shutdown is particularly concerning for the archive’s loyal users. Developers have stated it may be between two and four weeks before the site is fully operational again.   
 The outage is suspected to be the result of a hacking incident, and while volunteers at AO3 have assured they are now taking steps to defend against future attacks, this prolonged shutdown has raised questions about the archive’s long-term viability. Between increasingly frequent maintenance issues, cybersecurity vulnerabilities and aging servers, we may need to start accepting a sad reality: AO3 is dying.  
 This is not the first time that the archive has been the target of a cyber attack. In July 2023, AO3 was the victim of a distributed denial-of-service attacks, also known as a DDoS, by a group targeting “anti-Muslim activity,” according to Cyber Security Hub . At the time, AO3 claimed that it would implement measures to prevent another cyber attack of that caliber. Now, three years later, AO3 has fallen victim to another cyber attack despite their improved protections. AO3 has also not ruled out the possibility of a data leak as a result.  
 Major news organizations including The New York Times and CNN have since reported on the AO3 shutdown, particularly focusing on the reaction of loyal users of the platform. Fanfiction enjoyers have resorted to sharing Google Drive and epub links of previously saved works. Many have been loud in their refusal to resort to Fanfiction.net or Wattpad, as neither site offers the same streamlined tagging system, lack of censorship or lack of corporate agenda. 
 Digital communities, like AO3, are most vulnerable in our current corporatized landscape. Wattpad’s fall into a profitable corporation caused the site to face an onslaught of criticisms geared toward their updated terms of service that bans “not safe for work” content. However, AO3 has held fast to its commitment to be a free and uncensored site that fosters creativity, but this commitment has also left it vulnerable. Relying on donations and volunteers means that the archive cannot always utilize the newest or most updated technology, nor can it buy into high-end cybersecurity software to protect against attacks. 
 This is not an endorsement in favor of AO3 going the route of corporatization. Our digital landscape’s shift and the lack of protections for nonprofit creative spaces as well as our lack of funding for creative spaces will continue to erode AO3 until the site can no longer support itself. I previously wrote a CT article about my concerns surrounding commercialization of Wattpad, but without AO3 as a worthy alternative, I wonder if there can be a future for writers and creatives if we cannot hold onto the one home we have for boundless artistic pursuits.  
 So, what can we do? Save the works you publish on a separate drive and donate to the archive whenever you can. The site promotes semi-regular fundraising efforts, the money you put toward AO3, or other nonprofit creative-run spaces furthers their longevity. Corporatization will continue to infect sites committed to providing free and accessible creative content, but our efforts can stave off the untimely end.  
 Platforms like Wattpad will continue to flourish and pull in substantial profit while AO3 withers and eventually dies out. As a reader and publisher to the site, I do not want to see AO3 die out, but unless we fight against corporate hostility, AO3 will continue to fight a losing battle. We should take the time we have, however much, to enjoy the last days of the platform against corporatization. Let us revel in the beauty of the uncensored fandom culture we have now, finite as it may be.  
 Editor’s Note: Since the time of writing, AO3 is up and running once again. For now.
